THE ABSTRACTION PROBLEM

A campaign is a number
and a rendering.

The case statement leads with square footage, bed count and a construction timeline. So does everyone else asking that donor for money this year. None of it tells anybody what actually changes.

The change is on the floor. It is the nurse who has worked that unit for nineteen years. The parent who drove ninety minutes each way, twice a week. The physician who can name exactly what she cannot do in the building she has.

None of that is in a rendering. We go and get it, and we bring it back in a form your whole campaign can use.

SOUND FAMILIAR?

Common problems we see

01

The case statement reads like a budget

Square footage, bed count and a timeline. Accurate, approved, and it moves nobody who is not already giving.

02

The gala film is a scramble

Somebody records three interviews the week before on a borrowed camera, and everyone in the room can tell.

03

The board has seen the renderings

They approved the project. They still cannot tell the story to a single person outside the room.

04

Postings do not fill clinical roles

Your best recruiters are the people already on the unit, and not one of them is on camera anywhere.

THE TIMING

The people who make the case are working today.

The nurse who has been on that unit for nineteen years retires. The family whose child came through moves away. The physician who can name what the building costs her takes a job somewhere else.

A campaign runs for years. The voices that make it land are only available now.

TERMS

The things we guarantee.

First cut in fourteen days or you do not pay.

Fourteen days after we leave, the first cut is in your hands. A day late and the project is free and you keep everything. Only that first cut carries a date, and its clock pauses on your approvals.

Nobody appears without a signed release.

On your forms or ours, whichever your compliance team prefers. If a participant changes their mind afterwards, they come out of the film, the cuts and the library at no charge.

We work around the floor, not the other way round.

Interviews are scheduled to clinical operations and moved when the floor needs them moved. No set is built in a corridor and no patient care is delayed for a camera.

QUESTIONS

A few things worth knowing.

Who decides who we interview?

You do. You know which patient, which nurse and which donor carries the story, and we do not. Give us the names and we handle everything after that.

How do you handle patient consent?

A signed release before anyone is on camera, on your forms if your compliance team prefers them. Nothing is filmed, edited or published without one, and a participant who withdraws later comes out of every deliverable at no charge.

What exactly is a quote library?

Every usable line from every interview, transcribed, attributed and sorted by theme. Your writers stop scrubbing through footage looking for the sentence they half remember.

Can one project serve the campaign and recruiting?

Yes, and most should. The same interviews carry both, because the reason someone gives and the reason someone stays are usually the same reason.

Do you need our facilities or crew?

Neither. We bring the crew, the lighting and the sound, and we work in the rooms you already have.

What if the campaign timeline slips?

It usually does, and it does not affect the footage. Interviews filmed now are just as usable at the kickoff, the gala and the close, which is why the timing argument runs the other way.
